verdicts.trueWording: Martin's readers and viewers can safely “have their chivalric cake and eat it too”
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (200, browser UA). Burt: “George R. R. Martin’s Westeros, however, offers up continual blood-soaked hypocrisy. Enamoured of noble houses, dragons, and titles, thrilling at the poisonings, rapes, and betrayals that undermine any noble goals, Martin’s readers and viewers can safely ‘have their chivalric cake and eat it too’ (p. 237).” Quote exact; the cited phrase is Roberts's (p. 237) as the claim says. The 'no sentence-level prose judgment' limb holds: this is the ONLY Martin passage in the whole review (grep for Martin/Westeros/Thrones returns just this sentence plus a bare 'Game of Thrones, both books (1996-?) and TV' date mention). Page adds 'dragons' to the noble-houses-and-titles list; byline Stephanie Burt, article published_time 2026 — both as the source field states.

verdicts.trueWording: suffers from one-dimensional characters and less than memorable imagery
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (200). Riskind excerpt: “Still, to my mind, this opening installment suffers from one-dimensional characters and less than memorable imagery.” Quote exact; Washington Post and 1996 both on the page. ⚠ Source-field date is wrong: the page credits “John H. Riskind, The Washington Post, June 28, 1996”, not 28 Jul 1996. That date is bibliographic metadata, not a limb of the claim sentence, so the grade stands — but the roundup's own title is 'The Original Reviews of George R.R. Martin’s A Game of Thrones'.

verdicts.trueWording: like all proper serials it gives the reader no emotional respite
verdicts.note: Live URL 403s to curl even with a browser user agent (route 1 failed); recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20250810124603id_/... (route 2, 200). Page: “And like all proper serials it gives the reader no emotional respite, ending with several razor-sharp question marks as the heavy wheels of fate groan into motion, and the murders and assassinations mount.” — credited “New York Times, Dana Jennings”. Quote exact; both limbs (no emotional respite; razor-sharp question marks) on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: not one of those literary writers who does seven drafts
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (200); full post text present, not paywalled. Church: “Martin’s writing is well above average for commercial prose, but he’s not one of those literary writers who does seven drafts; revision intensity of 2-2.5x, plus the work of hired editors, should suffice.” Quote exact; both limbs supported. Byline Michael O. Church, Jun 19, 2025, title 'The Tragedy of George R. R. Martin' — matches the source field.

verdicts.trueWording: the editing does not really begin until I deliver the finished novel
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture fetched (200, 2025-04-16 snapshot of westeros.org SSM Entry 998, dated February 29, 2000). First paragraph: “I do send them sections as I go along -- not individual chapters but sizeable chunks -- but the editing does not really begin until I deliver the finished novel. At which point they read the book and give me notes, and I revise.” Quote exact; the 'editors read it and give him notes' limb is the next sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: a copyeditor, who checks it for grammar, syntax, spelling, internal consistancy
verdicts.note: Same page/paragraph as 559. “Then the manuscript goes to a copyeditor, who checks it for grammar, syntax, spelling, internal consistancy, and the like, and flags any mistakes.” Quote exact including Martin's misspelling 'consistancy'; 'among other things' is the page's 'and the like'.

verdicts.trueWording: I revise constantly as I go along, always honing and polishing
verdicts.note: Same page, third body paragraph (as the page field says). “I have heard the same tales as you of writers who submit chapter one while still writing chapter two, but I could never work that way. I revise constantly as I go along, always honing and polishing.” Quote exact; the 'rather than submitting finished chapters serially' limb is the preceding sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: new idea while writing chapter fifty two ... change chapters three, nine, and twenty-one
verdicts.note: Same page, third body paragraph. “I may get a new idea while writing chapter fifty two which requires me to go back and change chapters three, nine, and twenty-one.” Quote exact; page writes 'fifty two' unhyphenated, claim writes 'fifty-two' — the claim's own rendering, outside the quoted span.

verdicts.trueWording: The repeated phrase she tried to cut back on in A Dance With Dragons
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture of Pajiba fetched (200, 2024-11-26 snapshot); full article text present. Numbered highlight 6: “The repeated phrase she tried to cut back on in A Dance With Dragons was ‘words are wind’ (which appears 14 times) but Martin was ‘stubborn.’” Quote exact; the editor is identified earlier as “George R.R. Martin’s editor, Anne Groell”, relaying her Suvudu Q&A — exactly as the claim frames it.

Same page, highlight 6. Quote exact, curly quotes and parenthetical included. Both limbs (the phrase; 14 occurrences in A Dance With Dragons) on the page. Pajiba is relaying Groell, and the claim correctly says 'Pajiba reports'.

verdicts.trueWording: two weeks to do the initial edit ... most of which was back-checking
verdicts.note: Same page, numbered highlight 7 (as the page field says): “She took two weeks to do the initial edit on A Dance With Dragons, most of which was back-checking information from previous books.” Quote exact; both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Three battles were cut from A Dance With Dragons for length and for writing time
verdicts.note: Same page, numbered highlight 2 (as the page field says). Quote exact and the full sentence carries both stated reasons — 'for length and for writing time'.

Same page, highlight 6, same sentence as 563/564. Quote exact. 'Stubborn about KEEPING the phrase' is carried by the page's own adversative construction — the phrase she tried to cut back on ... but Martin was 'stubborn' — so the limb is supported by the sentence, not merely inferred from context.

verdicts.trueWording: I always knew they were summer snows ... I knew that right from the beginning
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched live (200). The line is the post's pull-quote heading, printed directly under the title 'George R. R. Martin on the Architect and the Gardener / April 16, 2019' and repeated at the head of the body: “I always knew they were summer snows. Why did I know that? But I knew that right from the beginning.” Quote exact; the 'from the beginning' limb is the heading's own third sentence, and the body identifies the material as 'this MoPOP oral history clip'.

verdicts.trueWording: he fills this simple concept with so much poetic imagery
verdicts.note: Same page, body: “But what really struck me is Martin’s philosophy on the two types of writers and how they differ in approaching the work. In classic Martin fashion, he fills this simple concept with so much poetic imagery it’s almost like listening to a parable.” Quote exact; the two-types-of-writers limb is the preceding sentence. Minor: it is the third body paragraph after the heading quote, not the fourth.
